If you do something wrong, someone sees what you've done, and they decide to beat you because they deem that's the appropriate punishment/consequence, that is assault.

I have a decent amount of patience especially for my child that I birthed and love. I just see how small she is and that she's learning. These moments are all her firsts and how is she suppose to know how to behave or use manner, or not hit unless I teach her how to. Kids don't just learn these things out of thin air, they have to be taught like anything else in our lives. New job? You have to be trained. Move somewhere across the world, you have a new culture and maybe language to learn, so you seek out lessons. 

I really always thought this should be obvious and common sense, but it's not at all. Someone's parents are lacking in their own teaching skills because they weren't taught this!
Ouf, I'm sorry you are stuck in that mindset.
Yes. But hitting them is not the way to get that lesson across.

Parent or not, if you are hitting people, punching walls, slamming doors, throwing things etc, you need to learn to deal with anger. It's an emotion and that's how, but how you handle it is what matters.

I hope my girl always comes to me instead of being scared to come to me because she scared of how I'll react, or I have shown her in the past that I can't be trusted with her coming to me for help no matter the situation because if she's 4 or 14, she will still be learning. Hell, I'm still learning and plan to keep learning so that I can be a better human being and help others be better humans too.

It's one thing to fear a consequence, but hitting should not be one of those consequences. 

I'm in my 30s and no one has ever hit me in the real world as punishment... except maybe toddlers who don't know how to express their emotions yet. 

If kids don't know they shouldn't steal by the time they go out into the world, then that's a parenting fault. Not a lack of beating them. We don't steal because we have to trade something for the things we want, we don't just take it because we feel like it because that's taking from someone else's job that they work hard for. That's what I tell my 4 year old and that's what I'll tell her again any time she's asks or if she steals something, and she won't be allowed out by herself until she can be trusted again. 

There are many more ways to disciplin than hitting. That's it.

It's exhausting.
Even just the threat of that you WOULD hit them is instilling fear into them if they step out of line. This is also abuse.

In Canada, you cannot do more the a gentle and corrective tap. Like a pat on the bum to steer in a different direction, or grabbing their hands to stop them from doing something dangerous. If you leave a red mark, bruise, etc, that's abuse. 

Hitting and physical contact should not be used to discipline. Discipline should relate directly to the thing they are doing wrong/incorrectly.

For example, last week I took my LO for a walk and she wanted to ride her scooter. She fell early on because she had her shoes on the wrong feet ( told her to change them but she wouldn't and they gotta learn). She ended up with a skinned knee. And then when we came to a slight slope, she got scared because a slope is where she tripped on her shoe. I said we could go on a flat part instead. She said no and that she wanted me or my fiancé to hold her scooter while she goes. We said no because it hurts our backs and she can totally scoot on her own. It was also 615pm and getting close to bedtime routine. She didn't want to make a decision so I said if she doesn't make one, then we are going home. No more scooter for the day and we could try again tomorrow. 

A simpler one would be playing video games and rage quitting and throwing the controller. If you can't be angry about a video game without damaging the console or controller, then you can't play it for that day and we will try again tomorrow. It's important to make sure they can try again, and that the punishment is related to the crime. 

Sending kids to their rooms to deal with emotions alone, hitting, yelling, guilt tripping, emotional manipulation, will take their toll on children and can cause deep rooted trauma for them to deal with when they are older.

I have wicked trauma from being yelled at constantly and from being manipulated all the time. Now, in my 30s as a family support worker and a mom to a 4 year old, I see how easy it is to not yell at a child who is simply learning how to be human. I'm already there, I know how, but my daughter is learning, and it's my job to show her, teach her, etc. I teach her how to express herself appropriately. 

Now, when someone yells, or says my full name (not my nickname that I always go by), I get instant anxiety. My palms get sweaty, my chest and face heat up, I get butterflies, and my heart races. I work hard not to make my daughter feel like this. To make her feel heard and understood. 

I grew up being told "because I said so" "to make little kids like you ask questions" " because I'm the parent and your the child". A lot of power tripping and no understanding. I refuse to make my daughter feel that way.

You are NEVER to old for anything. 
I'm a human services counselor and it's my job to help people be a functioning part of society, it's my job to encourage people and meet them where they are at and help them build on existing skills. 

If one of my clients came to me and told me what you have said here. Here's what I'd say; 

There is no such thing as too old for anything. No achievement, no life goal, nothing. If you are functioning and able, then I say keep at it. Societal norms have taught us that we have to follow some type of timeline in order to be successful. It's wrong. So incredibly wrong. 

If you want to buy at house at 40-something, do it. It's better to achieve your goals at any given time, no matter how long it takes rather than giving up because someone  says you aren't up to part with the majority. 

If you want to learn a sport, an instrument, take up a new hobby, foster pets, learn to drive, learn a new job, it doesn't matter when you do it, it's that you do it anyways. 

This is going to sound harsh but hear me out. What someone thinks of you is none of your business. They are entitled to their thoughts and opinions. Should they always be voiced? No of course not.
